index: BMWP / ASPT (Biological Monitoring Working Party score per taxon)
note: Family-level sensitivity scores for freshwater benthic macroinvertebrates, the indicator group OneAquaHealth's field protocols put first for urban streams. Scores run from 1 (tolerant of pollution) to 10 (only in clean, well-oxygenated water). bmwp is the family score of the original BMWP (Armitage et al. 1983); ibmwp is the Iberian adaptation (Alba-Tercedor et al. 2002) as tabulated in the Spanish ministry's protocol (MAGRAMA 2011). Both were checked against the tables distributed with the biomonitoR R package. null means that index does not score the family: it is still recorded, and still feeds the One Health rules (mosquito larvae, snail hosts), but adds nothing to that index. These are screening scores, not a Water Framework Directive classification, which requires a standardised sample by a trained assessor. plain_name and look_for exist so a citizen never has to type a family name. Families a citizen cannot realistically tell apart from a phone photo are grouped to the level that is honest.

families.look_for: Two long tails, two claws on each foot, flat body under stones in fast water. Wing pads on the back.
families.means: Stoneflies need cold, clean, fast water with lots of oxygen. They are the first to disappear when a stream is polluted.

families.look_for: Two tails, patterned yellow-and-brown back, under stones in riffles.
families.means: Very sensitive to pollution and low oxygen.

families.look_for: Very thin, roll-shaped body, two short tails; looks like a tiny brown needle.
families.means: Clean, well-oxygenated water only.

families.look_for: Two tails, stout brown body, legs held out sideways.
families.means: Sensitive, but tolerates a little more than other stoneflies.

families.look_for: Three tails, very flat body, head wider than long, gills along the sides; clings to the top of stones.
families.means: Needs clean, well-oxygenated water.

families.look_for: Three tails, sturdy body, gills folded like plates over the back.
families.means: Sensitive to pollution and silt.

families.look_for: Three tails, forked feathery gills along the sides.
families.means: Sensitive; typical of clean streams with leaf litter.

families.look_for: Three tails, tusks on the head, feathery gills curved over the back; digs into sand and silt.
families.means: Needs oxygen in the sediment as well as the water.

families.look_for: Three tails, very small, a pair of square gill covers like a shield on the back.
families.means: Moderately sensitive; copes with some silt.

families.look_for: Three tails, slim streamlined body, darts in short bursts like a small fish.
families.means: The toughest mayflies. Common even in streams under some pressure.

families.look_for: Bright green caterpillar-like grub with no case, a hook at the tail end.
families.means: A predator of fast, clean riffles.

families.look_for: Grub with no portable case but feathery gills underneath; lives in a silk net between stones.
families.means: Copes with extra nutrients from sewage or run-off. Lots of these and nothing else suggests nutrient pollution.

families.look_for: Grub inside a tube case built from sand grains, twigs or leaf pieces.
families.means: Moderately sensitive; common in streams in fair condition.

families.look_for: Slim case of sand or plant material; very long antennae.
families.means: Sensitive to pollution.

families.look_for: Smooth, slightly curved case of fine sand grains.
families.means: Sensitive; clean streams with stable gravel.

families.look_for: Caseless grub in a loose silk net or tube among stones and plants.
families.means: Moderately sensitive.

families.look_for: Case of sand with two larger stones ballasted on the sides.
families.means: Sensitive; fast clean water.

families.look_for: Very smooth, hard, slightly curved sand case.
families.means: Sensitive.

families.look_for: Tiny hard-shelled beetle with long claws, walking slowly on stones; adults stay underwater.
families.means: Riffle beetles live underwater as adults and need steady oxygen, so they favour streams in fair-to-good condition.

families.look_for: Smooth oval beetle that swims in jerks and surfaces tail-first for air.
families.means: Breathes air, so it is not a good oxygen indicator; middling sensitivity.

families.look_for: Shiny black beetles spinning in circles on the water surface.
families.means: Middling sensitivity; needs slack water at the edge.

families.look_for: Domed beetle that surfaces head-first, antennae breaking the surface.
families.means: Middling sensitivity.

families.look_for: Flattened side to side, curls into a C, scuttles sideways under stones and leaves.
families.means: Needs reasonable oxygen and calcium. Common in healthy and moderately impacted streams alike.

families.look_for: Small lobster shape with large pincers, hiding under stones or in bank holes.
families.means: Native crayfish are sensitive to pollution and to crayfish plague carried by introduced species.

families.look_for: Lobster shape with hooks on the front legs of males; red swamp crayfish are deep red with bright bumps on the pincers.
families.means: The American crayfish families are introduced across Europe, tolerate poor water, collapse banks by burrowing, and carry crayfish plague, which kills native crayfish.

families.look_for: Flattened top to bottom like a woodlouse, crawls rather than swims.
families.means: Tolerant of organic pollution and low oxygen. Dominance by hoglice is a warning sign.

families.look_for: Bowling-pin shape anchored to a stone in fast water, fans at the head, sways in the current.
families.means: Filters food from fast water and copes with nutrient pollution. Some species bite people and livestock.

families.look_for: Thin worm-like larva, often bright red, wriggling in figure-eights in silt.
families.means: Red bloodworms carry haemoglobin so they survive very low oxygen. Finding almost only these means the stream is under heavy organic pressure.

families.look_for: Hangs head-down from the surface film in still water, dives with a wriggle when disturbed.
families.means: Breeds in still, warm, nutrient-rich water. This matters for people's health directly: mosquitoes spread disease, and they are the disease carriers OneAquaHealth tracks in urban streams.

families.look_for: Fat grey grub with no obvious head and a star-shaped breathing plate at the tail.
families.means: Middling sensitivity; lives in wet banks and leaf packs.

families.look_for: Small dark segmented larva in the film on stones in slow, dirty water.
families.means: Strongly associated with sewage and organic sludge.

families.look_for: Pale grub with a long thin breathing tube like a tail.
families.means: Breathes surface air through its tail, so it survives water with almost no oxygen. A strong pollution signal.

families.look_for: Thin red or pink worms, often in tufts waving out of soft black mud.
families.means: The classic sign of organic pollution and oxygen-poor sediment.

families.look_for: Soft flattened body that stretches and loops; suckers at both ends.
families.means: Tolerant of pollution.

families.look_for: Broad flat leech, often carrying young underneath.
families.means: Tolerant of pollution.

families.look_for: Pointed spiral shell, opening on the right when the tip points up.
families.means: Tolerant. Some pond snails host parasites that cause swimmer's itch in people.

families.look_for: Glossy thin shell, opening on the left when the tip points up.
families.means: Very tolerant of pollution and warm water.

families.look_for: Flat coiled shell like a rope coil.
families.means: Tolerant. Some ramshorns host human and livestock parasites.

families.look_for: Tiny cap-shaped shell stuck flat to a stone in flowing water.
families.means: Needs flow and oxygen; moderately sensitive.

families.look_for: Half-round patterned shell with a flat door, on stones.
families.means: Moderately sensitive.

families.look_for: Tiny pale two-part shell, the size of a grain of rice, in sand and silt.
families.means: Tolerant of silt and nutrient pollution.

families.look_for: Large dark oval shell half-buried in gravel or sand.
families.means: Moderately sensitive and slow to recover; many European species are threatened.

families.look_for: Soft arrowhead-shaped animal that glides smoothly over a stone, with two eyespots.
families.means: Middling sensitivity.

families.look_for: Long-legged bug skating on the water surface.
families.means: Middling sensitivity; lives on the surface film so it says little about the water below.

families.look_for: Swims upside down, rowing with long back legs.
families.means: Middling sensitivity; breathes air.

families.look_for: Swims the right way up, flat patterned back, oar-like back legs.
families.means: Middling sensitivity; breathes air, so it persists in low-oxygen water.

families.look_for: Slim nymph with three leaf-like tails and a very long first antenna segment.
families.means: Sensitive; needs clean flowing water with plants.

families.look_for: Slim nymph with three flat leaf-like tails.
families.means: Moderately sensitive.

families.look_for: Long-bodied nymph with no tail fins and a hinged grabbing jaw.
families.means: Sensitive; a predator of well-vegetated clean water.

families.look_for: Squat hairy nymph covered in silt, in slow water.
families.means: Sensitive on the BMWP scale, though darters cope with warm still water.

families.look_for: Dark larva with seven pairs of feathery side filaments and one long pointed tail.
families.means: Tolerates silt and nutrient pollution.

families.look_for: Very small pointed shell with a door, often in huge numbers.
families.means: Tolerant. Includes the invasive New Zealand mud snail.

families.look_for: Small striped triangular mussel glued in clumps to hard surfaces.
families.means: Introduced almost everywhere in Europe; clogs intakes and changes the whole food web. Tolerant of poor water.
